# Generative models

After classification, I worked through four generative approaches: a variational autoencoder, pixel-space DDPM, DCGAN, and a latent diffusion MLP that reuses a VAE bottleneck [@kingma2014vae; @ho2020ddpm; @goodfellow2014gan; @radford2016dcgan].

::: {.callout-warning}
## Decision: why I judged generative outputs qualitatively

I did not compute FID or Inception Score. Claiming quantitative generative quality without those metrics would oversell the results. My conclusions about sample quality are qualitative, based on the PNG grids in `results/figures/`. That is a real limitation, and I keep it visible on purpose.
:::

## VAE: compression and soft reconstructions

<p class="source-notebook">
<strong>Source notebook:</strong> <a href="https://github.com/jt-09/mnist-generative-models-lab/blob/main/notebooks/vae.ipynb">notebooks/vae.ipynb</a>
</p>

`vae.ipynb` trains a **16-D** VAE for **50** epochs. Final train / val loss: **100.22 / 100.09**.

Reconstructions preserve digit identity but look soft. Training curves show both losses settling near the same level.

::: {.fig-wide}
![VAE reconstruction grid comparing inputs and reconstructions](../assets/ext/figures/07_vae/reconstructions.png){fig-alt="Grid of original MNIST digits and their VAE reconstructions, showing preserved identity with softer edges."}
:::

<p class="fig-followup">
Identity usually survives: a three still looks like a three. Sharpness does not. That is the compression tradeoff in visual form, the decoder is reconstructing from a small latent code, not copying pixels.
</p>

::: {.fig-standard}
![VAE training and validation loss curves over epochs](../assets/ext/figures/07_vae/training_curves.png){fig-alt="Line plot of VAE train and validation loss across training epochs, converging near 100."}
:::

<p class="fig-followup">
The vertical axis is loss; the horizontal axis is epoch. Train and validation stay close (**100.22 / 100.09**), which is reassuring for overfitting, but the absolute scale is less important here than the qualitative reconstruction look.
</p>

::: {.hrt-block}
**Hypothesis:** A 16-D VAE would learn a usable latent space and reconstruct digits cleanly enough to look sharp at a glance.

**Result:** Train / val loss **100.22 / 100.09**; reconstructions keep class identity but look soft.

**Interpretation:** The VAE optimizes a reconstruction term plus a KL term that keeps the latent distribution close to a prior. That second pressure is useful, it makes the latent space regular enough to sample from, but it also encourages the decoder toward safer, blurrier averages when the latent code cannot store every stroke detail. With only 16 dimensions for a 28×28 image, the bottleneck is doing real compression. Soft edges are therefore not just a training failure; they are what you often get when you ask an ELBO-trained decoder to rebuild digits from a small code. The useful product of this notebook, for the rest of the lab, is less “pretty samples” and more “a latent space I can reuse.”

**Takeaway:** Compression and sharpness pull in opposite directions; a VAE can be valuable even when its reconstructions are not crisp.
:::

## Pixel-space DDPM: denoising in 784-D

<p class="source-notebook">
<strong>Source notebook:</strong> <a href="https://github.com/jt-09/mnist-generative-models-lab/blob/main/notebooks/ddpm.ipynb">notebooks/ddpm.ipynb</a>
</p>

`ddpm.ipynb` trains a pixel-space DDPM with **T=300** timesteps and a U-Net denoiser for **15** epochs. Average loss at epoch 15: **0.0454**.

::: {.fig-standard}
![DDPM training loss curve](../assets/ext/figures/08_ddpm/loss_curve.png){fig-alt="Line plot of DDPM average training loss across epochs, ending near 0.0454."}
:::

<p class="fig-followup">
Loss trends downward to about **0.0454** by epoch 15. That is a training signal, not a perceptual quality score.
</p>

::: {.fig-wide}
![Grid of digits generated by the pixel-space DDPM](../assets/ext/figures/08_ddpm/denoising_grid.png){fig-alt="Grid of MNIST-like digit samples generated by a pixel-space DDPM model."}
:::

<p class="fig-followup">
The samples are readable digits. The important engineering lesson for me was cost and dimensionality: the model is learning to denoise in the full 784-D pixel space across hundreds of timesteps.
</p>

::: {.hrt-block}
**Hypothesis:** Pixel-space diffusion would produce coherent digits and feel like the cleanest generative formulation, even if training was slower than a VAE.

**Result:** After 15 epochs, average loss **0.0454**; the sample grid shows recognizable digits.

**Interpretation:** DDPM learns to reverse a noise process step by step. Conceptually that is elegant: no adversarial game, no explicit encoder bottleneck in the generative path. Practically, every denoising step operates on the full image. On 28×28 that is still manageable, but it made the later motivation for latent diffusion obvious. If denoising is expensive here, it will be worse on larger images. I also had to keep myself honest about metrics: a falling noise-prediction loss means the denoiser is improving at its training objective, not that I have a calibrated perceptual score.

**Takeaway:** Pixel-space diffusion is a clear teaching model for the math, and a clear argument for moving the diffusion into a smaller latent space.
:::

## DCGAN: sharper samples, trickier optimization

<p class="source-notebook">
<strong>Source notebook:</strong> <a href="https://github.com/jt-09/mnist-generative-models-lab/blob/main/notebooks/dcgan.ipynb">notebooks/dcgan.ipynb</a>
</p>

`dcgan.ipynb` trains a DCGAN for **50** epochs. Final generator / discriminator losses: **3.41 / 0.32**.

::: {.fig-wide}
![DCGAN generated digit samples and loss history](../assets/ext/figures/09_dcgan/generated_digits.png){fig-alt="Grid of DCGAN-generated MNIST digits alongside training loss history for generator and discriminator."}
:::

<p class="fig-followup">
Many samples look sharper than my VAE reconstructions. The loss pair (**3.41 / 0.32**) is not a balanced fairy tale; it is a reminder that adversarial training is a moving target.
</p>

Latent interpolation suggests local smoothness in the generator’s latent space:

::: {.fig-standard}
![Latent space interpolation between DCGAN samples](../assets/ext/figures/09_dcgan/latent_interpolation.png){fig-alt="Rows of digit images showing smooth-ish transitions from interpolating in the DCGAN latent space."}
:::

<p class="fig-followup">
Interpolations are not perfect morphs, but neighboring codes often produce related digit shapes. That is qualitative evidence of local structure, not a formal manifold proof.
</p>

::: {.hrt-block}
**Hypothesis:** An adversarial generator would produce sharper digits than the VAE decoder, at the cost of less stable training dynamics.

**Result:** After 50 epochs, G/D loss **3.41 / 0.32**; samples look usable and often sharper; interpolations are locally coherent.

**Interpretation:** The discriminator pushes the generator away from blurry averages that can satisfy a pure reconstruction loss. That pressure is why GANs can look crisp. The downside is co-training: the generator and discriminator chase each other, so the loss numbers are harder to read than a VAE ELBO or a diffusion MSE. I would not call this run “stable training” in a strong sense, but the saved outputs are good enough to show the tradeoff I cared about, sharpness versus optimization drama. The interpolation panel then checks a second property: whether nearby latent vectors map to related images. They mostly do, which is what I want if I think of the generator as defining a usable sampling map.

**Takeaway:** Adversarial training can buy sharpness, but I have to monitor the game instead of trusting a single loss curve.
:::

## Latent diffusion MLP: compress first, diffuse second

<p class="source-notebook">
<strong>Source notebook:</strong> <a href="https://github.com/jt-09/mnist-generative-models-lab/blob/main/notebooks/latent_diffusion_mlp.ipynb">notebooks/latent_diffusion_mlp.ipynb</a>
</p>

::: {.callout-note}
## Decision: why latent diffusion made sense after pixel DDPM

Pixel-space DDPM made the math clear and the cost obvious. Diffusing in a VAE latent space keeps the denoising idea but moves it into 16 dimensions instead of 784. That is the engineering motivation: compress first, then run the expensive iterative process where each step is cheaper.
:::

The notebook trains a VAE, extracts latents, then trains a class-conditioned `LatentDiffusionMLP` for **150** epochs. I cite MSE **0.224** at epoch 150 to match the saved notebook write-up and README. The extracted metric JSON rounds this to **0.225**.

VAE reconstructions inside this notebook (separate from `vae.ipynb`):

::: {.fig-wide}
![VAE reconstructions from the latent diffusion notebook](../assets/ext/figures/10_latent_diff/vae_reconstructions.png){fig-alt="Grid of VAE reconstructions produced inside the latent diffusion notebook pipeline."}
:::

<p class="fig-followup">
These reconstructions set the ceiling for what latent diffusion can decode. If the VAE softens digits, the diffusion model cannot invent sharpness the decoder never learned.
</p>

Diffusion samples in latent space, decoded back to pixels:

::: {.fig-wide}
![Digits sampled from the latent diffusion MLP](../assets/ext/figures/10_latent_diff/diffusion_samples.png){fig-alt="Grid of MNIST-like digits generated by latent diffusion in VAE latent space and decoded to images."}
:::

<p class="fig-followup">
Samples are recognizable. They also inherit the VAE’s softness. That coupling is the central lesson of this notebook.
</p>

::: {.hrt-block}
**Hypothesis:** Diffusing in VAE latent space would be more practical than pixel-space DDPM while still producing readable digits.

**Result:** Latent diffusion MSE about **0.224** after 150 epochs; decoded samples are readable but inherit VAE blur. (Metric JSON rounds to 0.225.)

**Interpretation:** The pipeline has two stages with different jobs. The VAE defines a compressed coordinate system and a decoder. The diffusion MLP learns to denoise in that coordinate system, optionally with class conditioning. Because each diffusion step happens in 16-D rather than 784-D, the iterative process is cheaper per step. The catch is inheritance: sample quality is bounded by what the decoder can render from latent codes. Soft VAE reconstructions earlier in the notebook are therefore not a side plot, they are a diagnosis of the generative ceiling. I also duplicated VAE training between `vae.ipynb` and this notebook, which was convenient while learning and poor engineering hygiene for a real pipeline.

**Takeaway:** Latent diffusion is a systems idea as much as a model idea: move computation to a smaller space, and accept that you inherit the autoencoder’s limits.
:::

## How I think about the tradeoffs

I did not run controlled ablations, so this is personal takeaway from the PNGs and training runs:

| Family | What I noticed |
|--------|----------------|
| VAE | Usable latent space; soft reconstructions |
| Pixel DDPM | Clear math; heavy in pixel space |
| DCGAN | Sharper samples; trickier optimization |
| Latent diffusion | Efficient denoising path; quality capped by VAE |

No FID or IS, so none of this is a ranked generative leaderboard.
